n: Isaiah 9 begins with hope after the darkness of chapter 8. The northern regions of Zebulun and Naphtali (around Galilee) were the first to suffer Assyrian invasion, but their gloom will not last. The Book of Mormon reads “the Red Sea” where the KJV has “the sea” — a puzzling difference scholars still discuss.

f.g: Galilee, a region with many non-Israelites.

n: The people walking in darkness have seen a great light. Matthew applies this to Jesus beginning His ministry in Galilee — the very region first darkened by conquest.

God has multiplied the nation and increased its joy — like the joy of harvest or of dividing the spoils of victory. The Book of Mormon reads “increased the joy,” where the KJV text says “not increased the joy,” matching what many translators now prefer.

f.w: according to the joy in harvest

n: God has broken the oppressor’s yoke and rod, as He did in Gideon’s victory over Midian.
Warriors’ boots and blood-soaked garments will be burned as fuel — the end of war itself.

One of the most beloved messianic prophecies: a child born, a son given, who will govern. His titles — Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace — declare His divine nature. Latter-day Saints see Him as Jesus Christ.

f.w: unto us a child is born

f.g: Christ is “Father” as Creator and as the father of those born again through Him.

n: His government and peace will grow without end on David’s throne, established in justice forever. The Lord’s own zeal will accomplish it.
Now Isaiah returns to the northern kingdom: the Lord has sent His word against Jacob/Israel.
All will know it, including Ephraim and Samaria, who speak in pride and stubbornness.
Their boast: “The bricks fell? We’ll rebuild with cut stone. The sycamores were cut down? We’ll plant cedars.” They treat God’s warnings as a chance to build bigger, refusing to repent.

f.g: Common fig-mulberry trees used for cheap lumber, vs. costly cedar.

n: So the Lord will raise Rezin’s enemies against Israel and join their foes together.

f.g: Assyria and others opposed to Syria’s king.

n: Syria from the east and Philistines from the west will devour Israel. The refrain returns: His anger is not turned away; His hand is still stretched out.

f.w: his hand is stretched out still

n: Even after being struck, the people do not turn to the God who disciplines them.

f.w: turneth not unto him that smiteth them

n: So God will cut off head and tail, palm branch and reed — high and low — in a single day.

f.g: Palm branch (the top) and reed (the bottom) — the high and the lowly.

n: The “head” is the elders and nobles; the “tail” is false prophets who teach lies.
The leaders mislead the people, and those who follow them are destroyed.

f.w: the leaders of this people cause them to err

n: Even the young men, orphans, and widows — usually objects of God’s compassion — will share in the judgment, because hypocrisy and wickedness have spread to all. The refrain repeats.

f.g: Folly here means moral wickedness, not just foolishness.

n: Wickedness itself burns like a wildfire, consuming briers, thorns, and thickets until smoke rises in columns. Sin destroys from within.
Through God’s wrath the land is scorched. The people become fuel, and no one spares even his brother.

f.w: no man shall spare his brother

n: Starving and never satisfied, they consume one another — even their own kin. Civil strife eats the nation alive.

f.w: the flesh of his own arm

n: Manasseh and Ephraim, brother tribes, fight each other, and together turn against Judah. Still His anger is not turned away; His hand is stretched out still.

f.g: The two tribes descended from Joseph.
